name: Payables and Receivables
blurb: Invoice handling, credit risk, settlement, collections and working capital.
title: Payables and Receivables
answer: Invoice handling, credit risk, settlement, collections and working capital.

sections.body: Payables and receivables covers the money a business owes and is owed, from invoice receipt and coding to customer credit decisions, settlement, collections, and working capital timing. Artificial intelligence in this area is not a single system but a set of pattern recognition and prediction tools applied to documents, payment histories, and transaction flows. Invoice capture and coding systems read supplier bills, extract line items, and assign general ledger codes with human review on exceptions. Customer credit risk models score buyers from payment behavior and external data to set limits and terms. Programmable settlement and escrow uses rules and smart contracts to release funds when agreed conditions are met, while collections tools prioritize outreach and suggest payment plans based on past responsiveness.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The most mature work is in invoice capture and coding, where optical character recognition and language models now handle common invoice layouts with high accuracy, though unusual formats and complex allocations still need manual correction. Customer credit risk scoring is widely used but remains limited by thin data for small or new buyers and by the fact that past payment behavior does not capture sudden distress. Programmable settlement and escrow works for simple, well defined triggers such as delivery confirmation, but real world disputes, partial performance, and legal holdbacks often fall outside automated rules. Collections and payment plan tools can rank accounts and draft messages, but they do not reliably predict which customers will actually pay, and they cannot replace negotiation or legal escalation. Working capital timing models can forecast cash gaps, yet their accuracy depends on clean data and stable payment cycles, which many finance teams do not have.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Invoice Capture and Coding to see how raw supplier documents become structured accounting entries, since that is the foundation for everything downstream. From there, Customer Credit Risk explains how the same structured data and payment history feed decisions about who gets credit and on what terms. Programmable Settlement and Escrow moves from deciding terms to enforcing them, showing where automated release of funds can replace manual approvals. Collections and Payment Plans then covers what happens when settlement does not occur on time, including prioritization and structured repayment offers. Finally, Working Capital Timing ties the whole cycle together by showing how delays in any of the earlier steps change cash inflows and outflows, and where forecasting can help a business plan around those gaps.
